question.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability on an Unbounded Interval
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069722/assets/f25b8fea7403579d1ee40cc00b9447e3362dc28c2e9d41f762f51df5e11daaf8.png)

For a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ we have the following symmetry property for $a>0:$

$$
P(Z>a)=P(Z<-a)=Φ(-a)
$$

We're given that $Z∼N(0,1),$ and we wish to compute $P(Z>2.31).$ The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069722/assets/a3e01ca4fd737cea9afe95374a17c0428f83a6717d98a7557222a856aa2d0c02.png)

By symmetry, this equals the area corresponding to the probability $P(Z<-2.31).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069722/assets/ce206061194e357b9cd75f9b260e4035a8600726a17cc0ee04ab39219bd45e94.png)

Therefore,

$$
P(Z>2.31)=P(Z<-2.31)=Φ(-2.31)=0.0104.
$$

\begin{aligned}P(Z<-0.73) & =P(Z>0.73) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.73) \\  & =1-Φ(0.73) \\  & =1-0.7673 \\  & =0.2327.\end{aligned}

question.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability on a Bounded Interval
question.worked_solution:
We're given that $Z∼N(0,1),$ and we wish to compute $P(-0.18<Z<0.18).$ The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069722/assets/061aec33cb30172ec64c89841fc70cb2e5bec9b89f92ef0427ff9673bfa99219.png)

By the definition of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z),$ 

$$
P(Z\le z)=Φ(z).
$$

So, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.18<Z<0.18) & =P(Z<0.18)-P(Z\le -0.18) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.18)-P(Z\le -0.18) \\  & =Φ(0.18)-Φ(-0.18)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
Φ(-0.18)=0.4286,
$$

but we are not given $Φ(0.18).$ However, we can compute this using symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.18) & =P(Z\le 0.18) \\  & =P(Z\ge -0.18) \\  & =1-P(Z<-0.18) \\  & =1-P(Z\le -0.18) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.18) \\  & =1-0.4286 \\  & =0.5714\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.18<Z<0.18) & =Φ(0.18)-Φ(-0.18) \\  & =0.5714-0.4286 \\  & =0.1428.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability at a Point
question.problem: Given $X∼\text{Geom}(0.15),$ compute $P(X=7).$  Round your final answer to $4$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.15),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{(0.85)}^{x-1}(0.15), & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=7) & =f(7) \\  & ={(0.85)}^{6}(0.15) \\  & ≈0.0566.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.15),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{(0.85)}^{x-1}(0.15), & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<3) & =P(X\in {1,2}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\  & =f(1)+f(2) \\  & ={(0.85)}^{0}(0.15)+{(0.85)}^{1}(0.15) \\  & =0.2775.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Over a Bounded Interval Using the Complement
question.problem: Given $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{2}{3}),$ compute $P(X\ge 6)$ rounded to $4$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{2}{3}),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x-1}(\frac{2}{3}), & x=1,2,3… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X\ge 6.$ However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 6) & =1-P(X<6)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<6) & =P(X\in {1,2,3,4,5}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4)+P(X=5) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)+f(5) \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}(\frac{2}{3})+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}(\frac{2}{3})+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}(\frac{2}{3})+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}(\frac{2}{3})+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4}(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & ≈0.9959.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 6) & =1-P(X<6) \\  & ≈1-0.9959 \\  & =0.0041.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Estimating a Derivative Given a Graph Using a Central Difference Approximation: Word Problem
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069816/assets/1e11260301be8c0bb19a9fd47ffbbf71cc5fa4d94dbeae57af934b76fb17f0e1.png)

A particle has a speed of $v(t)$ meters per second after $t$ seconds. The graph of $v(t)$ is shown above. Approximate the rate of change of speed when $t=3$ using a central difference approximation with step size $h=1.$
question.worked_solution:
We use the central difference approximation

$$
{v}^{′}(x)≈\frac{v(t+h)-g(t-h)}{2h},
$$

 
at the time $t=2$ and step size $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{′}(2) & ≈\frac{v(3+1)-v(3-1)}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{v(4)-v(2)}{2} \\  & =\frac{3-1}{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of speed at the instant of time $t=2$ is approximately $1\,\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2}.$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Shift of a Horizontally Stretched Tangent or Cotangent Curve
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069862/assets/2f11d5b11c53f7b826291e0b7e95828f57d6f1242b768baf12c874be229b2935.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{5}+C),$ where $C$ is a constant. Given that $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2},$ what is the value of $C?$
question.worked_solution:
The parameter $C$ represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{5}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+\frac{5C}{3}$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{5}(x+\frac{5C}{3}))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{5}).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069862/assets/5e9b6568ec493d95db6fe72a6a19024326c5b920629e9ff44a85db54089aa2a6.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{5})$ by $\frac{\pi }{3}-0=\frac{\pi }{3}$ units to the right. Therefore:

$$
\frac{5C}{3}=-\frac{\pi }{3}\,⟹\,C=(-\frac{\pi }{3})(\frac{3}{5})\,⟹\,C=-\frac{\pi }{5}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $-\frac{\pi }{5}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $-\frac{\pi }{5}.$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch and Vertical Shift of a Transformed Cotangent Curve
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069862/assets/98edb404419e7ab515109f87addb44709513007b1a0105b648a3ce2b62ad547f.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(Bx)+D,$ where $B$ and $D$ are constants. What is $B+D?$
question.worked_solution:
The period $T$ of the function is

$$
T=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

The formula for the period $T$ of the function $y=A\operatorname{cot}⁡(Bx+C)+D$ is given by 

$$
T=\frac{\pi }{B}.
$$

Applying the formula of the period, we get

$$
\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{B}\,⟹\,B=\frac{\pi }{(\frac{\pi }{3})}=3.
$$

The parameter $D$ represents the vertical shift of the cotangent function. We see that the function has been translated by $1$ unit up. Hence, $D=1.$

Therefore, $B+D=3+1=4.$

Finally, the equation of the curve is

$$
y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x)+1.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Geometric Random Variable at a Point
question.problem: At an ice cream shop, on average, $25%$ of customers buy chocolate ice cream. What is the probability that the $4$th customer of the day is the first person buying a chocolate ice cream? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of customers that enter the ice cream shop until the first one buys a chocolate ice cream. Since the chance of a customer buying a chocolate ice cream is $25%,$ the number of customers before the first buys a chocolate ice cream can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=25%=\frac{25}{100}=0.25.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.25).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.25)^{x-1}(0.25) \\  & =(0.75)^{x-1}(0.25)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the $4$th customer of the day is the first buying a chocolate ice cream is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=4) & =f(4) \\  & =(0.75)^{4-1}(0.25) \\  & =(0.75)^{3}(0.25) \\  & ≈0.105\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Geometric Random Variable on a Bounded Interval
question.problem: A card is being randomly picked from a standard $52$ cards deck and put back in until getting a red card. What is the probability of choosing a red card within the first $5$ tries? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of cards picked until a red one is chosen. Since there are $26$ red cards in a $52$ cards deck, the chance of choosing a red card is $\frac{26}{52}.$ Thus, the number of chosen cards before getting a red card can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=\frac{26}{52}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.5).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.5)^{x-1}(0.5) \\  & =(0.5)^{x-1}(0.5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of choosing a red card within the first $5$ tries is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 5) & =P(X\in {1,2,3,4,5}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)+f(5) \\  & =(0.5)^{1-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{2-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{3-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{4-1}(0.5)+(0.5)^{5-1}(0.5) \\  & =(0.5)+(0.5)(0.5)+(0.5)^{2}(0.5)+(0.5)^{3}(0.5)+(0.5)^{4}(0.5) \\  & =[1+0.5+(0.5)^{2}+(0.5)^{3}+(0.5)^{4}](0.5) \\  & ≈0.969\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of a Leg Using the Pythagorean Theorem
question.problem:
A rocket that is launched vertically is tracked by a radar station located on
the ground $3\,\text{km}$ from the launch site. What is the vertical speed of the rocket at the instant when its distance from the radar station is $5\,\text{km}$ and this distance is increasing at a rate of $1\,000\,\text{km/h}?$
question.worked_solution:
We start by drawing a diagram of the problem.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069977/assets/7af033f137fd76e5e3003926a598e695f4e0852b11dc27dfa84d58040144972b.png)

In the diagram,

- $x$ is the distance between the radar station and the launch point,

- $y$ is the distance between the launch point and the rocket, and

- $z$ is the distance between the radar station and the rocket.

As shown in the diagram, $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ form a right triangle with $z$ as the hypotenuse. We wish to find the rate of change of $y,$ which is $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ 

We know that $x=3\,\text{km}$ and $z=5\,\text{km}.$ We can find $y$ using the Pythagorean Theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {3}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={5}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & =16 \\ y & =4\,\text{km}\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that:

- $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=1\,000\,\text{km}/\text{h},$

- the distance between the radar station and the launch point ($x$) remains the same, so $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=0.$

Finally, we differentiate both sides of ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ and then substitute in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({z}^{2}) \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(3)(0)+2(4)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2(5)(1\,000) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{10\,000}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =1\,250\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertical speed of the rocket is $1\,250\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Points at Which a Particle is Stationary Given the Acceleration Vector
question.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)⟩,\,0\le t<\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.
question.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to compute the velocity of the particle.

To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t,\int (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is stationary, we solve for the times at which the velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{2}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =0\,⇒\,t=0,\frac{\pi }{3}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\frac{1}{2} & =0\,⇒\,t=\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=\frac{\pi }{3},$ so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.
